notes.source: Edureka, "What is Google Cloud Platform (GCP)?" by Kislay Keshari

bullets.text: Google Cloud Platform runs on the same global infrastructure Google uses internally for Search, Gmail, and YouTube. It's organized geographically into regions (independent geographic areas) each containing multiple zones (isolated failure domains within that region).
You pick a region/zone based on three factors:
sub: Latency: put resources close to your users
Availability: spread across zones/regions so one outage doesn't take everything down
Durability: some services replicate data across zones or regions automatically

bullets.text: Google organizes its catalog into these groups:
sub: Compute — Compute Engine, App Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions
Networking — VPC, Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud CDN, Cloud DNS
Storage and Databases — Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore
Big Data — BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, Pub/Sub, Datalab
Machine Learning — Vertex AI, Vision API, Speech API, Natural Language API, Translation API
Identity & Security — Cloud IAM, Resource Manager, Cloud Security Scanner
Management and Developer Tools — Cloud Console, Cloud SDK, Deployment Manager

bullets.text: New accounts get a free trial credit for a limited period, a common way to explore services hands-on before committing to paid usage.

images: Choosing a Google Cloud compute option.png
notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "Where should I run my stuff?" by Priyanka Vergadia & Brian Dorsey, Jul 2021

bullets.text: Compute Engine (VMs you fully configure), GKE (managed Kubernetes clusters), Cloud Run (managed serverless containers), App Engine (fully managed serverless web apps), and Cloud Functions (single event-triggered functions).

bullets.term: Question 1: how much infrastructure control do you need?
bullets.text: If you need control over OS, disk images, CPU/RAM, or kernel-level settings, that points to Compute Engine, typical for legacy migrations or systems with a specific OS requirement. If your app is already containerized, GKE or Cloud Run are the two main paths.

bullets.term: Question 2: what's your actual workload shape?
sub: A simple HTTP-based app you want fully hosted → App Engine
A single function reacting to an event (HTTP, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage) → Cloud Functions
A containerized app needing HTTP/websocket support in any language → Cloud Run
An app needing a specific OS, custom network protocols, or hybrid/multi-cloud portability (via Anthos) → GKE
A legacy app with specific licensing/OS/kernel requirements (e.g. Windows apps, SAP HANA, genomics) → Compute Engine

bullets.term: Question 3: do you need open-source portability?
bullets.text: GKE, Cloud Run, and Cloud Functions are all built on open-source foundations (Kubernetes, Knative, and an open FaaS framework respectively), which avoids vendor lock-in and eases hybrid/multi-cloud moves.

bullets.term: Question 4: what are your team dynamics?
bullets.text: Small teams that want to focus purely on code lean toward serverless (Cloud Run, App Engine), no one has to manage infrastructure, scaling, or ops. Larger teams with their own CI/CD, security, and ops practices often prefer Compute Engine or GKE for full control.

Compute Engine and GKE bill per provisioned resource, you pay for what's running whether or not it's busy (offset by sustained/committed-use discounts). Cloud Run, App Engine, and Cloud Functions bill per request, pure pay-as-you-go.

notes.topic: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS vs CaaS
notes.source: Google Cloud, "PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS"

bullets.text: These four models sit on a spectrum of how much of the technology stack the cloud provider manages for you versus how much you're responsible for yourself. Less management responsibility generally means less low-level control, and the models aren't mutually exclusive, most real architectures mix several.

table.caption: Comparing the four service models
rows: You need full control, e.g. lift-and-shift migrations
You want container orchestration without managing bare VMs
You just want to ship code and let the platform run it
You need one small piece of logic to react to an event
You want a ready-to-use application with zero infra management

notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "Google Cloud Networking overview" by Priyanka Vergadia, Oct 2021

bullets.text: Google's network is organized into regions (round-trip time typically under 1ms between VMs within one) subdivided into zones, independent failure domains so one zone's outage doesn't take down another.
sub: Data center network: connects machines within a single data center
Private backbone WAN: Google's own private fiber linking data centers to each other
Public-facing WAN: where user traffic enters Google's network from the public internet

bullets.text: Traffic between two Google Cloud resources never has to leave Google's own backbone, it stays on Google's private fiber the entire way, which is part of why intra-Google-Cloud latency is so low.

sub: Cloud Interconnect — a dedicated physical line linking on-prem to a VPC
Cloud VPN — an IPSec tunnel over the public internet, cheaper but less consistent than Interconnect
Shared VPC — lets multiple projects share one network while staying logically separated (e.g. prod vs dev)
Cloud DNS — managed public and private DNS zones
Cloud Load Balancing distributes traffic across regions behind a single anycast IP
Cloud CDN caches content at Google's edge locations to cut latency and reduce load on the origin
VPC firewall rules — control instance-level traffic
Cloud Armor — defends HTTP(S) load balancers against DDoS and layer-7 attacks
Cloud NAT — lets private instances reach the internet outbound without needing a public IP
Cloud IAP (Identity-Aware Proxy) — replaces VPN-style network access with identity-aware, context-based access control
Traffic Director — a global service mesh control plane for microservices spanning more than one cluster
Service Directory — a real-time registry for discovering and connecting services across environments

notes.topic: Cloud Storage Buckets, Classes, and Lifecycle Rules
notes.source: Medium, "Google Cloud Storage Made Simple" by Nikhil Mogre, Jan 2026

bullets.text: Cloud Storage holds immutable objects inside buckets (not traditional folders/files). Buckets are globally unique and live in a region, dual-region, or multi-region. Uploading a file with the same name replaces the object rather than editing it in place.
A 99.9% SLA allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month; 99.95% allows about 22 minutes. Higher availability commitments generally track with Standard storage in multi-region configurations.
Keeps prior versions of an object when it's overwritten or deleted, useful for recovering from accidental changes, though every retained version is stored and billed until you clean it up.

Enforces permissions purely through IAM at the bucket level and disables legacy per-object ACLs. This is the recommended default since it's simpler to audit and reduces the risk of accidental public exposure.
IAM is the modern, recommended access-control method (project or bucket level). ACLs are the legacy, object-level method, harder to manage at scale and generally discouraged for new systems.

Encryption at rest and in transit is on by default. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are available for extra control. Retention policies and object holds add a compliance layer that blocks deletion or overwrite for a set period, useful for legal hold or regulatory requirements.

table.caption: Storage classes by access pattern
rows: Highest storage cost, lowest access cost
Lower storage cost, moderate access cost

notes.topic: Object vs Block vs File Storage
images: Object storage vs block storage vs file storage.png
notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "A map of storage options in Google Cloud" by Priyanka Vergadia, May 2021

bullets.text: Stores binary/unstructured data as objects, each with an ID, metadata, and the actual bytes, no filesystem hierarchy underneath. Highly durable and available, works for any data type or duration.
sub: Standard: frequent access, regional/dual-region for high throughput, multi-region for global serving
Nearline: roughly monthly access
Coldline: roughly quarterly access
Archive: rarely accessed, years-long retention
Common uses: streaming video, serving images/documents, backups, disaster recovery archives

bullets.text: Data is split into fixed-size blocks with no metadata context, and mounted directly as a drive by the OS.
sub: Persistent Disk: attaches to Compute Engine/GKE, good for VM boot disks, shared read-only data, backups, and databases needing consistent performance
Local SSD: also block storage but ephemeral, tied to the VM's lifetime, used for the lowest possible latency (caching layers, scratch disks, flash-optimized databases)

bullets.text: A fully managed NFS-style shared file system for unstructured data. Supports concurrent access from many clients with predictable low latency. Fits workloads expecting a traditional shared filesystem, HPC, media processing, EDA, and app migrations.

notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "Your Google Cloud database options, explained" by Priyanka Vergadia, Aug 2021

bullets.text: Relational (SQL) suits structured data with a stable schema that needs ACID guarantees. Non-relational (NoSQL) suits large-scale, frequently-changing, or varied-shape data.

sub: Atomic — transactions are all-or-nothing
Consistent — the database stays structurally valid after every transaction
Isolated — concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other
Durable — committed changes survive failures

bullets.text: Non-relational databases are usually optimized for one specific access pattern and scale horizontally, often favoring eventual consistency, though Firestore is a notable exception, it offers strong consistency and ACID transactions even across shards.

table.caption: Relational options
rows: General-purpose apps (CRM, ERP, e-commerce) needing managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server
PostgreSQL-compatible, built for demanding enterprise workloads with much faster analytics performance
Global, strongly consistent, horizontally scalable, used for gaming, payments, global ledgers
Lifting Oracle workloads onto dedicated hardware as-is

notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "What is Cloud SQL?" by Priyanka Vergadia & Gabe Weiss, Sep 2021

bullets.text: A fully managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. It automates provisioning, storage scaling, backups, and offers built-in high availability and failover.
Pick a region/zone, size the machine type (CPU/memory) to fit the workload, and choose SSD or HDD storage depending on latency, IOPS, and cost needs.

sub: Automated backups with point-in-time recovery
High availability (targets a 99.95% SLA) — adds a standby that Cloud SQL fails over to automatically if the primary goes down
Cross-region read replicas — protect against a full regional outage
Storage auto-grow — expands automatically as usage nears capacity
Cloud SQL Insights — a free built-in tool for diagnosing query performance issues beyond basic monitoring

bullets.text: Database Migration Service (DMS) moves existing MySQL/PostgreSQL databases (on-prem, other clouds, or other GCP compute) into Cloud SQL with continuous replication for minimal downtime, connecting via IP allowlisting, a reverse SSH tunnel, or VPC peering.

Encryption at rest and in transit by default, SSL-only connections can be enforced, and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy gives a secure local connection method. Meets common compliance standards (SSAE 16, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA).
Cloud SQL as the transactional store, combined with BigQuery for analytics, Vertex AI for predictions, and Datastream/CDC to stream changes out in near real time.

notes.source: Google Cloud official documentation, "GKE cluster architecture"

bullets.text: A control plane and worker nodes. In Autopilot mode GKE manages both; in Standard mode GKE manages the control plane while you manage the nodes.

Runs the Kubernetes API server, scheduler, and core resource controllers, it's the single endpoint you interact with (via kubectl or direct API calls), and every cluster component acts as a client of it.

GKE stores cluster state either in etcd instances on the control plane VMs, or in Spanner outside the control plane, depending on configuration. Either way, the API server always exposes an etcd-compatible API.

Compute Engine VMs that run your Pods, each with a kubelet agent that talks to the control plane and manages container startup. Shielded GKE Nodes use a virtual TPM to cryptographically verify node identity at registration time.

bullets.term: Autopilot vs Standard, for nodes specifically
bullets.text: Autopilot fully manages node lifecycle, scaling, and OS (always Container-Optimized OS). Standard gives you control over machine types and node pool sizing, and lets you SSH into the underlying VM directly.
Deploy across multiple regions to protect availability if an Artifact Registry outage or regional issue disrupts cluster creation or upgrades in one location.

notes.source: Google Cloud official documentation, "About LoadBalancer Services"

bullets.text: A Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer causes GKE to provision a Google Cloud passthrough load balancer, either external (internet-facing, via a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer) or internal (VPC-only, via an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer).

sub: Local — preserves the client's source IP, only routes to nodes with a ready serving Pod. Required for weighted load balancing.
Cluster — allows traffic to any node, may hop internally to another node (adds latency), and loses the original client IP.

bullets.text: External only. Distributes new connections in proportion to how many ready Pods each node has. Requires externalTrafficPolicy: Local and a supported GKE version.
Internal only. Prefers routing to node backends in the same zone as the client, reducing cross-zone traffic and cost, falling back to another zone if no healthy Pod exists locally.

For internal LoadBalancer Services, groups node endpoints into per-Service network endpoint groups (NEGs) instead of one shared instance group, scaling past the older 250-node backend limit. On by default in newer GKE versions, and can't be turned off once enabled.
Under Cluster policy, any node with at least one serving Pod anywhere in the cluster passes. Under Local policy, only nodes with a healthy, non-terminating Pod for that specific Service pass.

notes.source: Google Cloud official documentation, "Introduction to partitioned tables" (BigQuery)

bullets.text: Splits a large table into segments based on a chosen column, so a query filtering on that column can prune irrelevant partitions and scan less data, improving both performance and cost predictability.

sub: To scan only part of a table instead of the whole thing
To work around standard table size/row quotas
To get an accurate cost estimate before running a query
To use partition-level features: automatic expiration, writing to a single partition, or deleting a partition without a full table scan
Integer-range — buckets by numeric ranges you define
Time-unit column — based on a DATE/TIMESTAMP/DATETIME column, hourly/daily/monthly/yearly granularity
Ingestion-time — based on when BigQuery received the row, exposed via the _PARTITIONTIME pseudocolumn
Daily (the default): fits data spread across a wide date range
Hourly: high-volume data concentrated in a short window (under ~6 months)
Monthly or yearly: a small amount of data per day spread across a very wide range, especially when rows across many dates get updated frequently

bullets.text: Prefer clustering (or combine both) when you need finer-grained sorting than partitioning allows, queries filter on multiple columns, a column has high cardinality, or partitioning would create too many tiny partitions.
One table per day with a date-suffixed name forces BigQuery to track separate schema/metadata and check permissions per table, overhead that partitioning avoids entirely.

notes.source: Medium, "Hidden Gems of BigQuery — Part 4: Five types of Views" by Artem Nikulchenko, May 2023

bullets.text: All five let you query pre-defined SQL without re-writing it, but they differ sharply in storage cost, freshness, and how much you control refresh timing.

A base table can be referenced by at most 20 materialized views, aggregates must be the outermost operation, and outer joins plus non-deterministic functions aren't supported, so they don't fit every query shape.

table.caption: The five view types compared
rows: Re-runs the full underlying query every time, so it re-bills the full scan cost each query
Automatic, only for an identical repeated query on unchanged data, no setup, no cost guarantee
As fresh as the last scheduled run
You control the schedule; downstream users query the resulting table directly
Refreshed automatically (~5 min after a change, at most every 30 min)
BigQuery decides when to refresh, updates incrementally, and merges in live deltas even between refreshes
A newer opt-in variant for query shapes that don't qualify for standard incremental materialized views

notes.source: Medium, "Getting started with GCP #1" by Sarah, Mar 2024

bullets.text: Organization at the top, then optional Folders (which can nest), then Projects, then individual resources. Every resource belongs to exactly one project.

sub: Project ID — permanent, globally unique, human-readable, used to reference the project almost everywhere
Project Name — mutable, chosen by you, doesn't need to be unique
Project Number — assigned automatically by GCP, immutable

bullets.text: Let teams delegate administrative rights and organize projects by department or function. Folders require an Organization node to already exist.

The root of the hierarchy, created automatically once you set up Cloud Identity or Google Workspace. Two notable default roles live here: Organization Policy Administrator (broad policy control) and Project Creator (controls who can spin up new projects).
Policies set at any level apply to everything beneath it. Powerful, but risky if a broad role gets granted too high up in the hierarchy.
Who can do what on which resource:
sub: Who — a Google/Cloud Identity account, service account, or group
What — an IAM role (a bundle of permissions)
Where — any node in the resource hierarchy; the resulting policy applies there and everything below
Primitive — Owner/Editor/Viewer/Billing Administrator, broad and project-wide, generally discouraged in production
Predefined — Google-managed, scoped to a specific service (e.g. an instance-admin role for Bigtable)
Custom — org- or project-level only, built to match a least-privilege model exactly

bullets.text: Give non-human identities (a VM, an application) their own credentials to interact with other GCP services, rather than relying on a real user's credentials.

notes.topic: GCP IAM: Roles, Policies, and Best Practices
notes.source: usage.ai Blog, "What Is GCP IAM? Roles, Policies & Best Practices" by Debesh Singh

bullets.text: Instead of granting permissions one by one, admins bind identities (users, groups, service accounts, or external federated identities) to roles that bundle related permissions together.

Because permissions inherit down the resource hierarchy (organization → folder → project → resource), a role granted at a high level quietly applies to everything underneath it, the single most common source of over-permissioned environments.

bullets.term: How an access check actually runs
sub: 1. Authenticate the identity
2. Collect every IAM policy attached to the resource and its ancestors
3. Aggregate all roles the identity holds
4. Evaluate any IAM Conditions
5. Grant access if at least one binding allows it and no condition blocks it

bullets.text: If any binding grants a permission, it's allowed. Standard bindings don't support an explicit deny, only Conditions can restrict on top of a grant.

Add context-aware restrictions on top of a role binding, an expiration timestamp, specific resource attributes, or request attributes. Useful for temporary contractor access or timed production windows without having to manually revoke access later.

Long-lived downloaded JSON keys are a major risk if leaked. The safer pattern is short-lived credentials, Workload Identity Federation for external systems, or service account impersonation instead of sharing keys.

sub: Enforce least privilege
Avoid primitive roles in production
Grant roles to groups rather than individual users
Double-check the hierarchy level before granting a role
Regularly audit service accounts and remove unused ones
Use IAM Conditions for anything temporary
Periodically review policies with the IAM Recommender or Policy Analyzer

notes.source: Medium, "Differences Between IAM and ACL in GCP" by Forever O., Oct 2024

bullets.text: Manages access broadly and centrally, defines roles and permissions across an entire organization or set of services, letting admins control access from one place using role-based access control.
Manages access narrowly, attached directly to an individual resource (a file, a Cloud Storage object, a network port), specifying exactly which users or systems can do what to that one object.

IAM operates at the level of a whole platform, service, or many resources at once. ACLs operate object-by-object, fine-grained but doesn't scale well if you have to configure permissions resource-by-resource.

Use IAM as the default, broad access-control layer across an organization or environment, and reserve ACLs for the rare case where one specific object needs a permission that differs from the IAM-level default. In Cloud Storage specifically, IAM plus Uniform Bucket-Level Access is the recommended modern approach; ACLs are legacy and harder to audit at scale.

notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "Data security in Google Cloud" by Priyanka Vergadia, Jul 2022

bullets.text: Google encrypts data before writing it to disk. Data is chunked, each chunk gets its own data encryption key, and each key is wrapped by a key encryption key. Updated chunks get fresh keys rather than reusing old ones, so compromising one key or gaining physical disk access alone isn't enough to read customer data.
All traffic to Google Cloud over the internet requires a properly terminated TLS connection, protecting data moving between your systems and Google's, or between two Google services.

Confidential VMs and Confidential GKE Nodes encrypt data even while it's actively being processed in memory, using hardware-based memory encryption where Google itself doesn't have access to the key. Builds on top of Shielded VM protections against rootkits/bootkits.

table.caption: Key management options, from most to least Google-managed
rows: Google-managed service, you hold the reference
Teams that want control without building key infrastructure
Dedicated FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware Google manages
An external key-management partner, outside Google entirely
Full custody, Google only holds a URI reference
Strictest trust requirements, key material never touches Google
Lowest-trust model; Google never stores it, but can't recover your data if you lose it

notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "Implementing observability for always-on Ecommerce experience" by Vikas Saini & Logan Vadivelu, Sep 2022

bullets.text: Logging captures raw event data from an application and its infrastructure. Monitoring turns that (and other telemetry) into actionable insight, dashboards, alerts, and trend analysis.

sub: Cloud Logging — collects logs from 150+ sources, supports search and alerting
Cloud Monitoring — metrics dashboards and a query language for spotting patterns
Error Reporting — groups and deduplicates errors by stack trace
Cloud Trace — distributed latency tracing across services
Cloud Profiler — continuous CPU/memory profiling in production

bullets.text: Deprecated; the open-source Snapshot Debugger is the suggested replacement for inspecting a running app's state without stopping it.

sub: Platform logs — service-level activity from Google Cloud itself
User-written logs — sent via agent, API, or client library
Component logs — a hybrid, with a different entry structure
Security logs — Cloud Audit Logs and Access Transparency

bullets.text: Entries flow through the Log Router, which uses sinks to send some or all logs to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, or dedicated log buckets, filtered by inclusion/exclusion rules, and from there can feed a SIEM/SOAR system for security analysis.

sub: Keep Data Access audit logs enabled for sensitive environments
Enable network-level logging (VPC Flow, firewall, DNS) for security visibility
Centralize logs into one project for easier review and tighter access control
Set retention periods based on compliance needs
Tier alerts by priority so teams aren't drowning in noise
Budget for the ongoing cost of storing and querying log data

notes.topic: DevOps and CI/CD on Google Cloud
notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "DevOps and CI/CD on Google Cloud explained" by Priyanka Vergadia, Dec 2021

bullets.text: Integrate code changes frequently (multiple times a day) rather than in one big batch, with every integration verified by an automated build, so problems surface early instead of compounding downstream.
Extends CI by packaging and preparing software for release. Strategies like blue/green or canary deployments reduce release risk and remove the need to hand-tune deployment scripts.

Apps are shifting to hybrid/multi-cloud, monoliths are splitting into microservices with different languages and lifecycles, and workloads are moving to serverless/containers/Kubernetes, all of which make manual, ad hoc deployment far riskier than before.

bullets.term: What a solid pipeline should trigger automatically
sub: Packaging source code
Automated unit and integration tests
Consistent build environments
Required approvals before production
Blue/green or canary rollouts

bullets.text: A fully managed CI/CD platform that imports source from Cloud Storage, Cloud Source Repositories, GitHub, or Bitbucket, runs each build step in its own container, and can produce artifacts like container images. Integrates with Binary Authorization so only trusted images reach production, and offers private pools for enterprise network/security requirements.
IDE tooling for writing, running, and debugging cloud-native apps, which then hands off to Cloud Build for the actual build, packages into Artifact Registry, and deploys to GKE or Cloud Run.
A managed, opinionated continuous-delivery service focused on making GKE deployments easier and more reliable, with built-in security controls that plug into an existing DevOps toolchain.

notes.source: Medium, "Cloud-Native Advantages of Moving Your ETL Process to Cloud Run" by Averi Kitsch, Dec 2019

bullets.text: Not every ETL workload justifies the complexity of Dataflow or Composer. If your logic is a modest SQL/shell/Python script and data volume isn't huge, running it as a container on Cloud Run keeps things simple while still gaining cloud-native benefits.

bullets.term: Why move ETL to Cloud Run
sub: Pay-per-use billing, charged only while processing, to the nearest 100ms
Automatic scaling, including down to zero
No infrastructure to manage
Built-in retry/fault tolerance

bullets.text: Standardizes how events/data move between producers and consumers, supports fan-in/fan-out patterns, and retries delivery for up to 7 days if a subscriber is briefly down.
Use instead of Pub/Sub when you specifically need rate limiting, deduplication, configurable retries, or scheduled dispatch, useful for controlling how fast data gets processed downstream.

Since Cloud Run doesn't support long-lived streaming protocols natively, a common pattern is Pub/Sub push notifications triggering a Cloud Run service per event, e.g. processing an uploaded image the moment Cloud Storage emits a notification.

Cloud Scheduler kicks off a nightly Cloud Run job, which reads data (e.g. files from Cloud Storage), fans work out via Cloud Tasks, and a second Cloud Run service processes each task. Watch out: Cloud Run has a maximum request timeout (15 minutes, default 5), so long batch jobs need to be chunked.

images: How to transfer your data to Google Cloud.png
notes.source: Google Cloud Blog, "How to transfer your data to Google Cloud" by Priyanka Vergadia, Apr 2021

bullets.text: Picked based on data size, available bandwidth, and whether the transfer is one-time or recurring.

bullets.term: Why a physical appliance can beat the network
bullets.text: Illustratively, moving a petabyte over a typical 100 Mbps line could take years, versus about 40 days with an appliance, bandwidth math matters at that scale.

table.caption: Four transfer paths
rows: Cloud Storage tools (Console, JSON API, gsutil)
Smaller transfers up to a few TB, run directly from your own machine or scripts; gsutil supports multi-threaded rsync-style and streaming transfers
Recurring or larger jobs into Cloud Storage from other clouds, on-prem, or between buckets, with scheduling, retries, and logging
Very large datasets where bandwidth is the bottleneck; a physical device (~40TB or ~300TB) you load and ship to Google
Automated scheduled loads directly into BigQuery from SaaS apps, other cloud storage, or warehouses like Teradata/Redshift

notes.source: Google Cloud official documentation, "Implement Datastream and Dataflow for analytics"

bullets.text: Streams change data (inserts, updates, deletes) from Oracle, MySQL, or PostgreSQL sources directly toward BigQuery, using change data capture (CDC) so you get near real-time visibility instead of slow, periodic batch exports.

bullets.term: When to add Dataflow into the mix
bullets.text: When you need more control than a direct Datastream-to-BigQuery path offers, custom transformation logic, or manually defining logical primary keys.

sub: 1. Datastream writes change files into a Cloud Storage bucket
2. The bucket sends Pub/Sub notifications about new files
3. A Dataflow job (triggered by those notifications) processes the files
4. Dataflow merges the changes into BigQuery tables

bullets.term: Pieces you need to wire together
bullets.text: A destination Cloud Storage bucket, Pub/Sub notifications enabled on that bucket, one or more BigQuery datasets (often a staging/log dataset plus a final merged dataset), Datastream connection profiles for source and destination, and a running stream plus Dataflow job to consume it.

The source database needs a firewall rule allowing Datastream's public IP ranges (or a private connectivity method), and CDC must be explicitly configured on the source database before Datastream can capture changes.

notes.source: "Demystifying Google Cloud Dataproc in 2025: The Practical Guide" (vendor blog)

bullets.text: Google's managed service for open-source big data frameworks, Spark, Hadoop, Flink, and Presto, removing the manual work of provisioning, configuring, and patching clusters yourself.

bullets.term: The key architectural difference from on-prem Hadoop
bullets.text: Dataproc decouples compute from storage by using Cloud Storage instead of HDFS, so clusters can be spun up per job and deleted afterward without losing data. This is what makes Dataproc clusters practical to treat as disposable/ephemeral.

sub: Master node — runs the Spark driver or YARN ResourceManager, HDFS NameNode, job history
Worker nodes — run NodeManager, HDFS DataNode, Spark executors
Secondary/preemptible workers (optional) — cheaper, interruptible extra capacity

bullets.text: Compares pending memory requested by jobs against available memory, scaling workers up or down accordingly. It doesn't support Spark Structured Streaming and can't scale all the way to zero, at least one node always remains.

Removes cluster management entirely, you submit a Spark batch job and the service provisions and tears down the execution environment automatically. Trades some customization and iteration speed for zero idle-VM cost, priced by Data Compute Units (DCU) instead of provisioned vCPUs.

bullets.term: Dataproc vs Dataflow, in one line
bullets.text: Choose Dataproc for existing Spark/Hadoop/Hive code with minimal changes and direct control over cluster config. Choose Dataflow for new Apache Beam pipelines that need autoscaling and dynamic load balancing, especially continuous streaming or complex windowed transforms.
Roughly $0.01 per vCPU-hour across all nodes in the cluster, billed per second with a one-minute minimum, on top of the underlying Compute Engine/disk/network charges.

notes.topic: The GCP Data Pipeline (Ingestion to BI)
notes.source: Medium, "The GCP Data Pipeline: From Raw Ingestion to Business Intelligence" by Antonella Blasetti, Nov 2025

sub: Batch — collect data over a period, then load it all at once (e.g. a Cloud Storage load job or the BigQuery Data Transfer Service)
Streaming — write data event-by-event as it's generated, for near-immediate analysis

bullets.text: Loading batch data into BigQuery is free; streaming inserts are not, a real factor when deciding which ingestion mode fits a given source.

bullets.term: Legacy databases need an extra step
bullets.text: You generally can't connect a legacy on-prem database directly for real-time streaming, a change data capture (CDC) tool watching the transaction log is needed, streaming those changes into Pub/Sub as events.

bullets.term: How much processing you need before landing in BigQuery
sub: No transformation needed → simple Pub/Sub-to-BigQuery subscription pushes messages straight into a table with no code
Light per-message validation/filtering → Pub/Sub Single Message Transforms, a lighter-weight, code-free option, routes anything unfixable to a dead-letter topic
Join, cleanse, or aggregate before landing → add Dataflow into the pipeline

bullets.text: Modern pipelines often send streaming data straight into BigQuery first, bypassing the traditional pattern of writing to an operational database and waiting for a nightly ETL job, turning hours of latency into seconds.

sub: Federated queries — hit live operational databases (Cloud SQL, Spanner, AlloyDB) directly, provided they're in the same location as the BigQuery dataset
External tables (BigQuery Omni) — query files sitting in GCS, S3, or Azure Blob Storage as if they were native tables
BigLake — extends this further, letting you apply BigQuery's row- and column-level security onto those external files, unifying a data lake and a warehouse under one security model

bullets.text: BigQuery has first-class support for JSON-shaped data via STRUCT and ARRAY columns, it isn't limited to strictly tabular relational data.

notes.source: InfoWorld, "Preview: Google Cloud Dataplex wows" by Martin Heller, Apr 2023

bullets.text: A data management and governance layer that unifies, discovers, and classifies data across storage systems without requiring you to physically move or duplicate it, working by harvesting and centralizing metadata.

sub: Automatic data discovery and classification across structured, semi-structured, and unstructured sources with a unified searchable catalog
Logical organization of data into domains via lakes and zones
Centralized security/governance and auditing across otherwise siloed data
Built-in data quality checks and automatic data lineage
A serverless exploration workbench (Spark SQL, Jupyter notebooks) for querying governed data directly
Domain-centric data mesh — each business domain owns a Dataplex lake and controls its own data
Data tiering — a raw zone (accessible to engineers) feeds a curated zone (accessible to analysts and data scientists) as data matures
1. Raw CSV/JSON lands in Cloud Storage
2. Discovery extracts schema and does light curation into queryable Parquet/Avro/ORC using Dataflow and Spark
3. Spark SQL transforms and secures the data into BigQuery with access-controlled views
4. Business-ready data products come out the other end
Attribute Store — build taxonomies and attach policy attributes to tables or columns
Automatic data profiling — reveals statistical characteristics per column
Sensitive-data classification — DLP-style detection helps flag and mask PII
Data quality scans — auto-recommend rules for nulls, duplicate IDs, or out-of-range values based on the profiled data

notes.source: Medium, "Analytics Hub - GCP's Data Exchange Solution" by Sudharma Mokashi, Dec 2022

bullets.text: BigQuery's data-sharing platform, built to make sharing large analytics-ready datasets, within an org or externally, cheaper and easier than older ad hoc sharing setups, while keeping proper auditing and governance in place.
It also gives access to Google-curated datasets you couldn't get any other way, like Search Trends or the Data Commons knowledge graph, alongside whatever your own organization publishes.

sub: Public — visible to any Google Cloud user
Private (default) — shared directly with specific people or a group
Within Organization — shared org-wide
Data Exchange — groups related listings together and connects publishers with subscribers
Listing — the actual reference to a specific published dataset
Data Publisher — creates and manages listings
Data Subscriber — searches for and links a listing into their own BigQuery project
Administrator (Analytics Hub Admin role) — manages the exchange itself
Publisher — adds and manages listings
Subscriber — browses and subscribes to listings
Viewer — can see listings without subscribing

bullets.text: A live-linked view into the publisher's dataset rather than a copied snapshot, so the shared data always reflects the source.

notes.source: Google Cloud official documentation, "Cloud Billing overview"

bullets.text: Every active project must be linked to a Cloud Billing account, or product usage stops working even if the usage would otherwise be free.

bullets.term: How a billing account is structured
bullets.text: It connects to a Google payments profile (the legal entity responsible for the bill) and a Google payments account (which actually holds the payment method and charging cycle).

sub: Self-serve / online — credit card or ACH, monthly or threshold-based automatic charging
Invoiced / offline — check or wire transfer, typically one invoice per month, requires eligibility
Postpay — charged monthly, or when a spend threshold is hit; standard for self-serve accounts
Prepay — deducted from a pre-loaded balance; used for specific products like the Gemini API
Billing reports and cost trend views
Budgets with spending alerts
Anomaly detection for unusual spend spikes
AI-assisted forecasting and recommendations through the FinOps hub
Spend cap budgets — automatically pause usage of specified services once a cap is hit
Committed use discounts (CUDs) — for predictable workloads in exchange for a usage commitment
Programmatic notifications — automate a response (like adjusting quotas) when a budget alert fires

bullets.text: Labels (key-value pairs) attached to resources flow into billing exports, letting you break down cost by team, environment, or project at a granular level in BigQuery-exported billing data.

notes.source: "MLOps on Google Cloud: Smooth Machine Learning Deployments" (vendor blog, SlickFinch), Jul 2024

bullets.text: Combines ML, DevOps, and data engineering practices to automate the full model lifecycle, data prep, training, deployment, and ongoing monitoring, rather than treating each stage as a manual, one-off task.
Google's unified platform for the ML lifecycle: training and deploying models (pre-built or custom), automated hyperparameter tuning, and real-time performance monitoring, all in one place.
An end-to-end pipeline framework with dedicated components for data validation (catching bad/inconsistent input data), transform (preprocessing), training, and serving.

Extends its general CI/CD role specifically into MLOps, letting you define a YAML pipeline that chains data preprocessing, training, testing, and deployment into one repeatable, version-controlled workflow.
Automatically retrains models as new data arrives, commonly scheduled or event-triggered through Vertex AI Pipelines, so a model doesn't quietly go stale as the world changes.

Tracks a deployed model's real-world performance to catch data drift, degradation, or anomalies, using Vertex AI Monitoring (accuracy/latency metrics with alerting), Cloud Logging, and Cloud Monitoring dashboards.

bullets.term: Supporting tools mentioned alongside core MLOps
sub: Kubeflow Pipelines — portable Kubernetes-based ML workflows
Cloud Functions — lightweight event-triggered automation steps
Artifact Registry — stores trained models and their dependencies

notes.source: Medium, "What is a Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD)? Mastering Window Functions in Streaming Data" by Bhavana Jaiswal, May 2025

bullets.text: Groups streaming events over time so you can aggregate, filter, or detect patterns, choosing the right window type affects both accuracy and cost.

Dimension table attributes (like a customer's address) that change infrequently and unpredictably. SCD handling preserves historical accuracy as those values change over time, a separate but related concern from choosing a streaming window.

table.caption: Five window types
rows: Fixed-size, non-overlapping, back-to-back blocks; each event in exactly one window
Simple periodic metrics, e.g. sales totals every hour
Fixed-size but overlapping (a size + a hop interval); one event can land in multiple windows
Smoother trend detection, e.g. a rolling average updating every few minutes
Anchored to each individual event, not clock time; a new window opens per event covering a lookback period
Precise per-event analysis like fraud or anomaly detection where exact timing matters
Groups by gaps of inactivity; a session ends once no new event arrives within a defined gap
User-behavior analysis like clickstreams or chat sessions
Emits data at specific fixed timestamps rather than event grouping
Periodic dashboard snapshots or exact scheduled pulls, e.g. daily revenue at midnight

notes.source: in28minutes, "GCP Load Balancers - GCP Certification Cheat Sheet"

bullets.text: Distributes user traffic across application instances in one or multiple regions. Fully distributed, software-defined, with health checking, autoscaling, and a single anycast IP for global reach. Also supports internal (VPC-only) load balancing.

The network layer moves raw bytes (IP), the transport layer governs reliability (TCP for reliability, TLS for secure TCP, UDP for speed over reliability), and the application layer is where most apps actually talk (HTTP/HTTPS for web/REST, SMTP for email). Latency-sensitive apps like gaming or live video skip ahead and talk UDP directly for performance.

sub: Backend — the group of endpoints (e.g. an instance group) receiving traffic
Frontend — defines the IP, port, and protocol clients connect to (an SSL certificate is required if terminating TLS there)
Host and path rules — HTTP(S) load balancing only, routes requests to different backends based on URL path, hostname, headers, or HTTP method

bullets.text: The external hop (client to load balancer) is typically HTTPS, while the internal hop (load balancer to VM, over Google's network) can safely drop to HTTP/TCP since that traffic never leaves Google's backbone.

table.caption: Load balancer types by traffic shape
rows: Global HTTPS web traffic across regions
Non-HTTPS TCP traffic needing SSL termination
Non-HTTP TCP traffic, no SSL offload needed
Lower-level traffic that doesn't need a proxy
Internal lower-level traffic, no proxy needed
